Corsaires d’Umbar

Les Corsaires d’Umbar sont les héritiers des rebelles gondoriens vaincus au terme de la Lutte Fratricide, mêlés aux anciennes populations d’Umbar et aux lignées númenóréennes établies depuis longtemps sur les rivages méridionaux. Leur identité est née de l’exil, de la défaite et d’une revendication persistante : celle d’incarner une tradition plus légitime que celle des souverains demeurés au Gondor.

Héritage et origines

Après la défaite de Castamir et de ses partisans, de nombreux rebelles trouvèrent refuge à Umbar. Ils y formèrent une aristocratie corsaire persuadée d’avoir été trahie par le Gondor. Leur hostilité envers le Royaume du Sud est nourrie par une mémoire dynastique, par le désir de revanche et par la conviction que leurs ancêtres furent privés d’un pouvoir qui leur revenait.

Apparence

Les Corsaires présentent une grande diversité d’apparences. Les lignées nobles conservent souvent des traits dúnedain : grande taille, cheveux sombres, port altier et longévité supérieure à celle des Hommes communs. D’autres familles sont davantage mêlées aux populations du Harad et aux marins du Sud.

Umbar

Umbar est une cité portuaire puissante, fortifiée et tournée vers la mer. Ses quais, arsenaux, chantiers navals et entrepôts forment le cœur économique et militaire de la Culture corsaire. Le pouvoir y est rarement stable et dépend des grandes maisons, compagnies maritimes, capitaines, armateurs, guildes et réseaux d’espionnage.

La mer comme voie de puissance

La mer leur fournit richesse, mobilité, prestige et vengeance. Leur maîtrise maritime couvre la navigation côtière et hauturière, le pilotage, la lecture des étoiles, la gestion des voiles et cordages, les débarquements, les abordages, le blocus et la guerre navale.

Navires et équipages

Les navires corsaires vont de la galère rapide au bâtiment de guerre lourdement armé. L’équipage forme une communauté soudée mais hiérarchisée. La discipline à bord est sévère, et le partage du butin suit des règles précises.

Société et hiérarchie

La société corsaire est fortement hiérarchisée. Les grandes familles dominent les institutions, contrôlent les flottes et possèdent les principaux domaines. Sous elles se trouvent capitaines, officiers, armateurs, marchands, maîtres artisans, soldats, marins, ouvriers, esclaves et captifs.

Noblesse et mémoire

Les familles entretiennent soigneusement leurs généalogies. Une ascendance réelle ou revendiquée peut justifier un commandement, un mariage, la possession d’un navire ou une revendication territoriale. Les ancêtres occupent une place presque sacrée.

Tempérament

Les Corsaires sont fiers, ambitieux, démonstratifs et farouchement attachés à leur réputation. Ils apprécient l’audace, l’intelligence tactique, la loyauté envers l’équipage, l’éloquence et le prestige. Leur sociabilité est brillante mais souvent calculée.

Haine du Gondor

Le Gondor demeure leur principal ennemi historique. Cette haine s’exprime par les raids côtiers, la prise de navires, l’espionnage, le soutien aux rébellions, les alliances avec les ennemis du Gondor et la propagande dynastique.

Relations extérieures

Leurs rapports avec les Númenóréens Noirs sont ambigus : ils partagent une partie de leur héritage et leur hostilité envers les Fidèles, mais se méfient de leur autoritarisme et de leur proximité avec l’Ombre. Ils commercent aussi avec les peuples du Harad, malgré un mépris et une méfiance réciproques.

Religion et funérailles

Leur religion mêle traditions gondoriennes déformées, héritage númenóréen du Sud, culte des ancêtres et pratiques locales. Certains honorent Námo, Varda, Ossë ou Uinen. Les funérailles des nobles et capitaines peuvent inclure l’exposition du corps, des chants funèbres, des offrandes, des armes et des maquettes de navires.

Langues

L’adûnaïque demeure prestigieux parmi les grandes familles et les érudits. Le westron et le haradaïque sont très répandus. Les marins et agents peuvent connaître le sindarin, le noir parler, l’apysaïque, le varadja et divers dialectes côtiers.

Vêtements, tatouages et armures

Ils portent des vêtements riches et voyants adaptés au climat chaud et à la vie maritime : lin, coton, soie, couleurs noires, rouges, pourpres, bleues, blanches et dorées. Les tatouages indiquent souvent un navire, une victoire, un équipage ou un serment.

Ils privilégient les armures permettant de se déplacer sur un pont : cuir, maille légère, brigandine, casques ouverts et protections partielles.

Armes et manière de combattre

Leur arsenal comprend épées, cimeterres, sabres, dagues, haches d’abordage, lances, hallebardes, arcs, arbalètes, javelots et gaffes. Ils excellent dans l’abordage, les combats sur les ponts, les raids nocturnes, les attaques de ports et les opérations amphibies.

Commerce, piraterie et course

La distinction entre marchand, corsaire et pirate est souvent floue. Un capitaine peut commercer durant une saison, escorter une flotte la suivante, puis attaquer un port ennemi dès que l’occasion se présente. La contrebande et l’espionnage font naturellement partie du commerce.

Professions et formation

Cette Culture favorise les Combattants, Roublards, capitaines, marins, pilotes, navigateurs, espions, diplomates, marchands, contrebandiers, ingénieurs navals, gardes, pirates et nobles exilés.

Place dans la création de personnage

La Culture des Corsaires d’Umbar convient à un personnage issu d’une grande maison exilée, d’un équipage corsaire, d’un chantier naval, d’une compagnie marchande, d’un réseau d’espionnage, d’une famille de capitaines ou d’une troupe de débarquement.

Elle peut être proposée comme Culture normale ou soumise à l’accord du MJ selon l’orientation de la campagne.

Langues de départ

  • Adúnaic — Parlée 8 / Écrite 6
  • Westron — Parlée 8 / Écrite 6
  • Haradaic — Parlée 8 / Écrite 6

Corsairs of Umbar

The Corsairs of Umbar are the heirs of Gondorian rebels defeated at the end of the Kin-strife, mingled with the older populations of Umbar and Númenórean bloodlines long established on the southern shores. Their identity was born from exile, defeat, and a persistent claim: that they embody a tradition more legitimate than that of the rulers who remained in Gondor.

Heritage and origins

After the defeat of Castamir and his supporters, many rebels found refuge in Umbar. There they formed a Corsair aristocracy convinced that Gondor had betrayed them. Their hostility toward the Southern Kingdom is nourished by dynastic memory, a desire for revenge, and the conviction that their ancestors were deprived of power that rightfully belonged to them.

Appearance

Corsairs show a great diversity of appearance. Noble bloodlines often preserve Dúnedain traits: tall stature, dark hair, proud bearing, and greater longevity than Common Men. Other families are more thoroughly mingled with the peoples of Harad and the sailors of the South.

Umbar

Umbar is a powerful fortified port city turned toward the sea. Its quays, arsenals, shipyards, and warehouses form the economic and military heart of Corsair Culture. Power there is rarely stable and depends on great houses, maritime companies, captains, shipowners, guilds, and spy networks.

The sea as a path to power

The sea provides wealth, mobility, prestige, and revenge. Their maritime expertise covers coastal and open-sea navigation, piloting, reading the stars, handling sails and rigging, landings, boarding actions, blockade, and naval warfare.

Ships and crews

Corsair ships range from fast galleys to heavily armed warships. A crew forms a close-knit but hierarchical community. Discipline aboard ship is severe, and shares of plunder follow precise rules.

Society and hierarchy

Corsair society is strongly hierarchical. Great families dominate institutions, control fleets, and own the principal estates. Beneath them stand captains, officers, shipowners, merchants, master craftsmen, soldiers, sailors, laborers, slaves, and captives.

Nobility and memory

Families carefully maintain their genealogies. Real or claimed ancestry can justify command, marriage, possession of a ship, or a territorial claim. Ancestors occupy an almost sacred place.

Temperament

Corsairs are proud, ambitious, demonstrative, and fiercely attached to their reputation. They appreciate boldness, tactical intelligence, loyalty to the crew, eloquence, and prestige. Their sociability is brilliant but often calculated.

Hatred of Gondor

Gondor remains their principal historical enemy. This hatred is expressed through coastal raids, capture of ships, espionage, support for rebellions, alliances with Gondor's enemies, and dynastic propaganda.

External relations

Their relations with Black Númenóreans are ambiguous: they share part of their heritage and hostility toward the Faithful, but distrust their authoritarianism and closeness to the Shadow. They also trade with the peoples of Harad despite mutual contempt and suspicion.

Religion and funerals

Their religion blends distorted Gondorian traditions, the Númenórean heritage of the South, ancestor worship, and local practices. Some honor Námo, Varda, Ossë, or Uinen. Funerals of nobles and captains may include lying in state, funeral songs, offerings, weapons, and models of ships.

Languages

Adûnaic remains prestigious among great families and scholars. Westron and Haradaic are widespread. Sailors and agents may know Sindarin, the Black Speech, Apysaic, Varadja, and various coastal dialects.

Clothing, tattoos, and armor

They wear rich and conspicuous clothing suited to a warm climate and maritime life: linen, cotton, silk, and colors of black, red, purple, blue, white, and gold. Tattoos often mark a ship, victory, crew, or oath.

They favor armor that allows movement on deck: leather, light mail, brigandine, open helmets, and partial protection.

Weapons and way of fighting

Their arsenal includes swords, scimitars, sabres, daggers, boarding axes, spears, halberds, bows, crossbows, javelins, and boat hooks. They excel at boarding, fighting on decks, night raids, attacks on ports, and amphibious operations.

Trade, piracy, and privateering

The distinction between merchant, corsair, and pirate is often blurred. A captain may trade during one season, escort a fleet the next, then attack an enemy port as soon as an opportunity presents itself. Smuggling and espionage naturally form part of commerce.

Professions and training

This Culture favors Fighters, Rogues, captains, sailors, pilots, navigators, spies, diplomats, merchants, smugglers, naval engineers, guards, pirates, and exiled nobles.

Place in character creation

The Corsair Culture of Umbar suits a character from a great exiled house, a Corsair crew, a shipyard, a merchant company, an espionage network, a family of captains, or a landing force.

It may be offered as a normal Culture or made subject to GM approval depending on the direction of the campaign.

Starting Languages

  • Adúnaic — Spoken 8 / Written 6
  • Westron — Spoken 8 / Written 6
  • Haradaic — Spoken 8 / Written 6

Heritage and origins

After the defeat of Castamir and his supporters, many rebels found refuge in Umbar. There they formed a Corsair aristocracy convinced that Gondor had betrayed them. Their hostility toward the Southern Kingdom is nourished by dynastic memory, a desire for revenge, and the conviction that their ancestors were deprived of power that rightfully belonged to them.

Appearance

Corsairs show a great diversity of appearance. Noble bloodlines often preserve Dúnedain traits: tall stature, dark hair, proud bearing, and greater longevity than Common Men. Other families are more thoroughly mingled with the peoples of Harad and the sailors of the South.

Nobility and memory

Families carefully maintain their genealogies. Real or claimed ancestry can justify command, marriage, possession of a ship, or a territorial claim. Ancestors occupy an almost sacred place.

Corsairs are proud, ambitious, demonstrative, and fiercely attached to their reputation. They appreciate boldness, tactical intelligence, loyalty to the crew, eloquence, and prestige. Their sociability is brilliant but often calculated.

Gondor remains their principal historical enemy. This hatred is expressed through coastal raids, capture of ships, espionage, support for rebellions, alliances with Gondor's enemies, and dynastic propaganda.

External relations

Their relations with Black Númenóreans are ambiguous: they share part of their heritage and hostility toward the Faithful, but distrust their authoritarianism and closeness to the Shadow. They also trade with the peoples of Harad despite mutual contempt and suspicion.

Adûnaic remains prestigious among great families and scholars. Westron and Haradaic are widespread. Sailors and agents may know Sindarin, the Black Speech, Apysaic, Varadja, and various coastal dialects.

Clothing, tattoos, and armor

They wear rich and conspicuous clothing suited to a warm climate and maritime life: linen, cotton, silk, and colors of black, red, purple, blue, white, and gold. Tattoos often mark a ship, victory, crew, or oath.

They favor armor that allows movement on deck: leather, light mail, brigandine, open helmets, and partial protection.

Their arsenal includes swords, scimitars, sabres, daggers, boarding axes, spears, halberds, bows, crossbows, javelins, and boat hooks. They excel at boarding, fighting on decks, night raids, attacks on ports, and amphibious operations.

The distinction between merchant, corsair, and pirate is often blurred. A captain may trade during one season, escort a fleet the next, then attack an enemy port as soon as an opportunity presents itself. Smuggling and espionage naturally form part of commerce.

This Culture favors Fighters, Rogues, captains, sailors, pilots, navigators, spies, diplomats, merchants, smugglers, naval engineers, guards, pirates, and exiled nobles.

The Corsair Culture of Umbar suits a character from a great exiled house, a Corsair crew, a shipyard, a merchant company, an espionage network, a family of captains, or a landing force.

It may be offered as a normal Culture or made subject to GM approval depending on the direction of the campaign.

  • Westron — Spoken 8 / Written 6
  • Haradaic — Spoken 8 / Written 6

Heritage and origins

After the defeat of Castamir and his supporters, many rebels found refuge in Umbar. There they formed a Corsair aristocracy convinced that Gondor had betrayed them. Their hostility toward the Southern Kingdom is nourished by dynastic memory, a desire for revenge, and the conviction that their ancestors were deprived of power that rightfully belonged to them.

Appearance

Corsairs show a great diversity of appearance. Noble bloodlines often preserve Dúnedain traits: tall stature, dark hair, proud bearing, and greater longevity than Common Men. Other families are more thoroughly mingled with the peoples of Harad and the sailors of the South.

Umbar

Umbar is a powerful fortified port city turned toward the sea. Its quays, arsenals, shipyards, and warehouses form the economic and military heart of Corsair Culture. Power there is rarely stable and depends on great houses, maritime companies, captains, shipowners, guilds, and spy networks.

The sea as a path to power

The sea provides wealth, mobility, prestige, and revenge. Their maritime expertise covers coastal and open-sea navigation, piloting, reading the stars, handling sails and rigging, landings, boarding actions, blockade, and naval warfare.

Ships and crews

Corsair ships range from fast galleys to heavily armed warships. A crew forms a close-knit but hierarchical community. Discipline aboard ship is severe, and shares of plunder follow precise rules.

Society and hierarchy

Corsair society is strongly hierarchical. Great families dominate institutions, control fleets, and own the principal estates. Beneath them stand captains, officers, shipowners, merchants, master craftsmen, soldiers, sailors, laborers, slaves, and captives.

Nobility and memory

Families carefully maintain their genealogies. Real or claimed ancestry can justify command, marriage, possession of a ship, or a territorial claim. Ancestors occupy an almost sacred place.

Temperament

Corsairs are proud, ambitious, demonstrative, and fiercely attached to their reputation. They appreciate boldness, tactical intelligence, loyalty to the crew, eloquence, and prestige. Their sociability is brilliant but often calculated.

Hatred of Gondor

Gondor remains their principal historical enemy. This hatred is expressed through coastal raids, capture of ships, espionage, support for rebellions, alliances with Gondor's enemies, and dynastic propaganda.

External relations

Their relations with Black Númenóreans are ambiguous: they share part of their heritage and hostility toward the Faithful, but distrust their authoritarianism and closeness to the Shadow. They also trade with the peoples of Harad despite mutual contempt and suspicion.

Religion and funerals

Their religion blends distorted Gondorian traditions, the Númenórean heritage of the South, ancestor worship, and local practices. Some honor Námo, Varda, Ossë, or Uinen. Funerals of nobles and captains may include lying in state, funeral songs, offerings, weapons, and models of ships.

Languages

Adûnaic remains prestigious among great families and scholars. Westron and Haradaic are widespread. Sailors and agents may know Sindarin, the Black Speech, Apysaic, Varadja, and various coastal dialects.

Clothing, tattoos, and armor

They wear rich and conspicuous clothing suited to a warm climate and maritime life: linen, cotton, silk, and colors of black, red, purple, blue, white, and gold. Tattoos often mark a ship, victory, crew, or oath.

They favor armor that allows movement on deck: leather, light mail, brigandine, open helmets, and partial protection.

Weapons and way of fighting

Their arsenal includes swords, scimitars, sabres, daggers, boarding axes, spears, halberds, bows, crossbows, javelins, and boat hooks. They excel at boarding, fighting on decks, night raids, attacks on ports, and amphibious operations.

Trade, piracy, and privateering

The distinction between merchant, corsair, and pirate is often blurred. A captain may trade during one season, escort a fleet the next, then attack an enemy port as soon as an opportunity presents itself. Smuggling and espionage naturally form part of commerce.

Professions and training

This Culture favors Fighters, Rogues, captains, sailors, pilots, navigators, spies, diplomats, merchants, smugglers, naval engineers, guards, pirates, and exiled nobles.

Place in character creation

The Corsair Culture of Umbar suits a character from a great exiled house, a Corsair crew, a shipyard, a merchant company, an espionage network, a family of captains, or a landing force.

It may be offered as a normal Culture or made subject to GM approval depending on the direction of the campaign.
